troubleshooting--B1-body--bandBatteryTip:
Your device’s battery life has been optimized to collect data for approximately 14 nights. 

Avoid having a critically low battery level before going to bed in order to record a full night of sleep data.

**What do the lights on my NC° Band mean?**

:b1-light-charging: Pulsating light: Connected and charging (full charge in about 2.5 hours)

:b1-light-full: Steady light: Battery fully charged
troubleshooting--B1-body--bandCare:
We’re here to help you look after your new device with a few quick tips: 

**Cleaning your sensors**

Keep the two sensors on the inside of your device clean by regularly wiping them with a soft, dry cloth. This will help ensure accurate readings. 

**Cleaning your band**

The nylon band is durable and easy to clean. You can simply wipe it down with a damp cloth as needed. Like any fabric, the band may show signs of wear with extended use.  

**Try not to get your device wet**

Your device is splash resistant, so it's fine to wear it while washing your hands but avoid submerging it in water (e.g., showering or bathing). We also recommend avoiding prolonged exposure to very hot or very cold temperatures. 

**Avoid scratches**

The device’s sensors are sensitive, so avoid contact with sharp objects or rough surfaces that could scratch them.

For more help, contact [Customer Support](https://help.naturalcycles.com/hc/en-us/requests/new?utm_source=NCApp).
troubleshooting--B1-body--bandDataUsage:
When you wear your device overnight, it records body temperature, heart rate and motion. 

**How is this data used?**
- Body temperature data is needed to calculate your fertility status
- Heart rate data helps us detect changes  (e.g. if you’ve slept differently or are unwell)
- Motion data ensures the device measures data only during sleep
troubleshooting--B1-body--bandInvalidDat:
The invalid data error can be displayed for a number of reasons. These include a sensor malfunction, an issue with data transfer or problems while measuring. 

To help us resolve this issue, please access your device’s diagnostic log available below.

Next, we’ll connect you with our Support Team. This will help us investigate the issue further and get things working for you again.
troubleshooting--B1-body--bandNotConnect:
If your NC° Band is not connecting to the Natural Cycles app on your iOS or Android device, it could mean that it is out of reach, out of battery or asleep. Please try the following troubleshooting steps:

1. Make sure your phone and NC° Band are close to each other
2. Plug your NC° Band into its charger
3. Turn off your phone’s Bluetooth and turn it on again
4. Open your NC° app again and let the app try to find your device automatically
5. If this fails, try connecting the NC° Band manually via the My Device page

Tip: Make sure you are connecting to the right NC° Band by checking that it’s serial number matches the one shown in your My Device > Device info page.

If you are still having issues, please [contact Customer Support](https://help.naturalcycles.com/hc/en-us/requests/new?utm_source=NCApp).
troubleshooting--B1-body--bandNotSyncing:
This can happen for a number of reasons, including your device running out of battery or not connecting to the app. 

We recommend wearing your device to bed with sufficient battery charge, checking the app and NC° Band are connected and that your device is fully set up.

If this problem persists, please [contact Customer Support](https://help.naturalcycles.com/hc/en-us/requests/new?utm_source=NCApp).

troubleshooting--R1-body--ringCare:
We’re here to help you look after your new device. Check out a few quick tips: 

**Protect it day-to-day**

NC° Ring is built for everyday wear, but you can still take some steps to protect it. Avoid contact with harsh chemicals or rough surfaces — especially metal — to keep your device looking and performing its best. 

**Cleaning your device**

Rinse under running water with a mild detergent. Take time to clean the inside of the device where the sensors are located. Dry thoroughly and leave to air for a few minutes before wearing again.

**Water & heat**

Your device handles showers and splashes (IPX7 rated), but avoid soaking for long periods. Keep away from heating pads, saunas, or direct sunlight when storing.

**Battery care**

Charge your NC° Ring regularly rather than running it to empty — battery lasts up to 14 days. A full charge takes about an hour. 

Tip: Turn on battery alerts to get notified when device battery is running low. 

For more help, [contact Customer Support](https://help.naturalcycles.com/hc/en-us/requests/new?utm_source=NCApp).
troubleshooting--R1-body--ringDataUsage:
When you wear your device overnight, it records body temperature and motion. 

**How is this data used?**
- Body temperature: This data is analyzed by our algorithm and is essential for calculating your daily fertility status.
- Motion data: This is used to detect movement and enables the device to track when you are sleeping.
troubleshooting--R1-body--ringNotConnect:
If your NC° Ring is not connecting to the NC° app, it may be out of reach, out of battery, or asleep. Please try these steps:

1. Place NC° Ring onto its charger
2. Turn Bluetooth off, wait 5 seconds, then turn it on again
3. Open your NC° app again and let the app try to find your device automatically
4. Try closing and re-starting the NC° app.

If the above doesn’t work, go to phone settings → Bluetooth — if you see NC° Ring listed, tap (i) → Forget this device.

If you are still having issues, please [contact Customer Support](https://help.naturalcycles.com/hc/en-us/requests/new?utm_source=NCApp).
troubleshooting--R1-body--ringNotSyncing:
There are several potential reasons why your temperature data might not be syncing to the NC° app, such as the device running out of battery, a connection failure with the app, or the device not being paired correctly before its first use.

We recommend wearing your device to bed with a sufficient battery charge, checking that the app and NC° Ring are connected, and making sure that your device is fully set up.

If this problem persists, please [contact Customer Support](https://help.naturalcycles.com/hc/en-us/requests/new?utm_source=NCApp).

tutorial-box-period-title: When is a period irregularly long?
tutorial-box-period-title-txt:
A period is considered a normal length if it’s up to 7 days long. 

Even if your period length is considered regular, it can be a good idea to track how heavy your period flow is too. If you have a very heavy flow, and it’s accompanied by other symptoms such as severe cramping or fatigue, there might be something else going on. In that case, consider contacting your healthcare professional.

If you choose to Go Anonymous, we can seperate your personal and fertility data in our database. You’re the only one with a unique key that links the two.

Note! Your data is always protected by NC° Secure, but this extra layer of identity protection makes it impossible for us to know who you are.

txt-cycle-phase-body--FOLLICULAR:
The follicular phase is the first half or so of your cycle. It starts with your period and ends with ovulation.

### What’s happening with hormones?

Your body will experience an increase in both estrogen and the follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) as your body prepares to release an egg. These hormones can make you feel more energetic and optimistic.

### How to make the most of this phase:
* Take advantage of your strength and energy by increasing the intensity of your exercise and challenging yourself physically. Remember to stay hydrated!
* Dive into creative tasks and tricky projects as your cognitive function can be peaking.
* Eat plenty of healthy fats and proteins to support hormone production.
* Notice if it’s easier to fall asleep — sleep patterns tend to be more stable in this phase.

### Follicular phase & the NC° algorithm

During this phase, your body starts to enter its fertile window. Your temperature will stay low until after ovulation.
txt-cycle-phase-body--LUTEAL:
The luteal phase is the second phase of your cycle, which starts after ovulation and ends with your period.

### What’s happening with hormones?

An increase in progesterone causes your temperature to rise — a sign that ovulation has occurred. Estrogen is generally lower than in the follicular phase. PMS symptoms can be caused by hormone fluctuations — mood swings, irritability, anxiety, and fatigue are common. Progesterone can make you sleepy, but PMS can cause restlessness. You might find yourself feeling more withdrawn or introspective. 

### How to make the most of this phase:
* Opt for moderate exercise, like biking, swimming, or strength training. If PMS symptoms are strong, low-impact activities like stretching or walking can be beneficial.
* Choose complex carbs (e.g., whole grains) to balance blood sugar levels.  This can help curb cravings for carbs or sweets that might intensify in this phase.
* Keep a consistent bedtime routine. Avoid heavy meals or caffeine before bed. 

### Luteal phase & the NC° algorithm

After ovulation, the algorithm predicts when you will get your period based on how long your luteal phase is. The length of this cycle phase tends to be more stable. We can send you reminders when PMS symptoms might hit, if you have this setting turned on.
txt-cycle-phase-body--OVULATION:
Ovulation is when one of your ovaries releases an egg. The egg travels down your fallopian tube and may become fertilized if it is met by a sperm cell within 24 hours. 

### What’s happening with hormones?

Estrogen is at its peak, and luteinizing hormone (LH) surges, triggering ovulation. This phase is often associated with optimism, confidence, and an increase in sex drive. You may feel more motivated, outgoing, and social.

### How to make the most of this phase:
* Your body is primed for physical challenges. Consider incorporating strength training, cardio, or high-intensity interval training (HIIT).
* To support the rise in energy, ensure a balanced intake of carbs, proteins, and fats. Include anti-inflammatory foods like berries and fatty fish to reduce inflammation.

### Ovulation & the NC° algorithm

Your “ovulation window” is the timeframe that our algorithm predicts when your ovulation is likely to happen. It then narrows down the window to identify the most likely day in your cycle. Your predicted ovulation day may change as more data is added, such as ovulation test results.
txt-cycle-phase-body--OVULATION_WAITING:
### What’s happening with hormones?

Once you’ve ovulated, progesterone levels rise, and this increases your body temperature. The egg cell can only survive for up to 24 hours once it’s released, so after that time you won’t be fertile again until your next cycle.

### Ovulation & the NC° algorithm

A consistently elevated temperature is needed for the algorithm to confirm that ovulation has occurred. This can take several days, or until the end of your cycle. Until it’s confirmed, you’ll have Red Days.
txt-cycle-phase-body--PERIOD:
### What’s happening with hormones?

During the menstrual phase, estrogen and progesterone levels are low. This is what triggers the shedding of your uterine lining — what you see as your period. You might also experience some fatigue or cramps. Mood swings and irritability are also common. As your period ends and estrogen starts to rise, you'll likely start to feel better.

### How to make the most of this phase:

* If you’re low on energy, stick with gentle exercise like walking or yoga.
* It’s normal to experience fatigue and/or cramps. Listen to your body and rest when needed. 
* Eat iron-rich foods (e.g., leafy greens, red meat, etc.) to replenish iron lost from your bleeding.
* Keep a consistent sleep schedule and try relaxation techniques if your sleep is disrupted due to cramping or discomfort.

### Your period & the NC° algorithm

Your period data is key for the algorithm to predict your cycle and your fertility better, so make sure to log it every day of your period. Your temperature is lower during this phase than after ovulation.
txt-cycle-phase-body--cycle-length:
### Why is cycle length important?

Cycle length, period length, and cycle length variation (a measure of how much the length of your cycle changes from cycle to cycle) are basic characteristics of the menstrual cycle. They can serve as important indicators of reproductive and overall health. 

Some variation is normal from cycle to cycle, but if the length of your cycle varies from your average by 8 or more days, it could be a sign of a medical condition, so it’s best to contact your healthcare provider.

### Cycle length & the NC° algorithm

Cycle length is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next period. The variation is the number of days you cycle length is likely to change from your average from cycle to cycle.

txt-irregular-modal-body--PERIMENOPAUSE:
Before perimenopause, we say something is considered irregular if it’s consistently outside the benchmarks listed below. Of course we expect things to change during this time, and that we will eventually stop cycling.

During perimenopause, we use these benchmarks as a way to let you know more concretely about broader patterns and changes to your cycle — since the transition likely won’t be a gradual straight line. 

Changes are expected, so these alerts might not be news to you. However, if you see a new pattern or feel that something isn’t right, contact your healthcare provider if you haven’t already. Remember to bring your Cycle Report so that you have more data to facilitate the conversation.

You might see the **Irregular** symbol if:

txt-perimenopause-assessment-info-bottom:
You can get one of the following results:

- *Not yet in perimenopause:* Your data suggests that you may not be experiencing perimenopause yet.
- *Early perimenopause:* This stage is often characterized by the presence of several symptoms, without significant changes to your cycle.
- *Mid perimenopause:* Irregular cycles, with variations of 8 or more days and cycle lengths below 21 or above 35 days, are typical of this stage.
- *Late perimenopause:* Cycles become less frequent and often longer, with average cycle lengths exceeding 60 days.
- *Not enough data:* We may need more information about your cycle history, or you may have indicated a possible condition whose symptoms can overlap with those of perimenopause.
- *Postmenopause:* No period for more than 12 months.

Your symptoms may change over time, and you might experience different symptoms at different stages of perimenopause.
txt-perimenopause-assessment-info-top:
## Stages of perimenopause

NC° Perimenopause is intended for general wellness and informational purposes. It is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease or medical condition. Always speak with a qualified healthcare professional about any medical concerns or questions.

### How this assessment is calculated

We analyze responses based on key factors:

- Age
- Cycle characteristics
- Symptoms and how much they affect your daily life
- Current scientific understanding of perimenopause experiences

txt-pmp-hormones-body--EARLY:
Progesterone is usually the first hormone to become more erratic and start dipping, which can shift your cycle and make PMS feel stronger.

Estrogen levels become somewhat less stable than before perimenopause, often slightly higher and fluctuating more. This can lead to heavier bleeding, mood shifts, and irritability.

Your cycle might still be quite regular, but ovulation can be more unpredictable. Shorter cycles, spotting, and breast tenderness are also common in this stage.
txt-pmp-hormones-body--LATE:
Both estrogen and progesterone are generally lower in this stage, although estrogen may still surge unexpectedly from time to time.

This can lead to more hot flashes, sleep disturbances, vaginal dryness, mood shifts, and emotional sensitivity.

Cycles tend to become longer and more irregular. The ovarian reserve is low by this stage, so ovulation can be infrequent and unpredictable.
txt-pmp-hormones-body--MENOPAUSE:
Menopause is your very last period, but it’s only confirmed once you've gone 12 months without a menstrual bleed. 
marking a new stable hormonal baseline.

In postmenopause, the big hormonal fluctuations quiet down as estrogen and progesterone stabilize at their new, lower levels. Many people begin to feel more grounded and more like themselves again

Symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, and brain fog often become less intense or less frequent over time. Some symptoms, like vaginal dryness, may continue, but they are highly treatable.
txt-pmp-hormones-body--MIDDLE:
Hormonal changes tend to be more noticeable in this stage. Estrogen starts to become more erratic, often with higher peaks and sharp drops. Progesterone continues to decline.

These shifting hormone levels can lead to some of the stereotypical symptoms that might impact your daily life. These include hot flashes, brain fog, mood shifts, and sleep disruption.

Irregular cycles, occasional skipped periods, and inconsistent ovulation are also typical in this stage.

Recovery after childbirth isn't linear — you'll most likely encounter highs and lows unique to your journey. 

Suffering complications during labor can leave you feeling frustrated, traumatized, and even powerless. It's okay to feel however you feel.

These are all completely normal and temporary emotions. With time, you will start feeling like yourself again. As you heal, NC° Postpartum is here to guide you through this crucial transitional phase.

txt-pregnancy-end-delivery-method-info-b:
A cesarean section can be an essential and lifesaving surgery, but it may mean your recovery time is a little slower.

What you are going through may feel new or even a bit uneasy, please know this is normal and we are here to help. 

NC° Postpartum supports you every step of the way with resources tailored to your journey.

When a delivery requires forceps, this can have a mental and physical impact on your body. These medical tools can often lead to a prolonged and more painful recovery. 

You might have had a more traumatic delivery, and we’re here for you. With the NC° Postpartum mode, we’ll provide guides and daily check-ins that support your recovery at every stage.

If your delivery method was a planned cesarean, you’re not alone. C-sections account for nearly a quarter of all childbirths globally, and their use continues to rise.

As common as they are, there can still be risks, such as a slower recovery time.

We’re here to help as you heal from your surgery and enter this next phase. 
NC° Postpartum provides you with resources and guides to support your recovery at every stage.

When a delivery requires a vacuum cup, it can affect you mentally and physically. The use of these medical tools can even lead to a prolonged and more painful recovery. 

We’re sorry you’ve experienced this, and we are here to help you as you heal. 
With the NC° Postpartum mode, we’ll provide guides and daily check-ins that support your recovery at every stage.

No two births are alike. Even when labor goes smoothly, the body will need time to heal. After vaginal delivery, it’s normal to feel sore, exhausted, and even overwhelmed.

We’re here to guide you through this transitional phase. 

NC° Postpartum gives you resources and guides to support your recovery journey.

There are many good reasons to try VBAC. Since it doesn’t require surgery, it can make recovery time faster and reduce the chance of infection. Even though the risks are low, this method can still affect you both physically and mentally.

NC° Postpartum supports you every step of the way with educational guides, daily health check-ins, and emotional support.

Breastfed, formula-fed, or both? How you feed your newborn is up to you. There’s no right or wrong way as long as babies get the nutrition they need. 

However, there is a link between breastfeeding and fertility return after birth. If you're breastfeeding, your ovulation might be delayed.

Knowing your feeding choice allows us to support your changing needs as your cycle gets back on track.

txt-pregnancy-end-goal-body-postpartum:
NC° Postpartum guides you through the physical and mental recovery of childbirth with resources tailored to support your overall health and well-being during this crucial transitional phase. 

Taking your temperature is not required in this mode, but measuring is encouraged as it helps our algorithm detect when your fertility returns so you can better prepare.

While NC° Postpartum is not intended to be used as birth control, it will give you a daily fertility status after postpartum week four. Still, until the app detects your ovulation, it will only display Red Days.
txt-pregnancy-end-goal-body-recovery: NC° Recovery is an interim mode of NC° Plan Pregnancy, where you can follow your body’s recovery without receiving a daily fertility status. The algorithm works the same, but we recommend this mode if you’re still experiencing physical and/or emotional symptoms of pregnancy loss.

txt-pregnancy-end-healthscore-info-body:
While recovery is different for everyone, highs and lows are expected as our hormones adjust after childbirth.

But how do you know if it’s too heavy and when you might need support?

We’re here to help. NC° Postpartum lets you track how you’re feeling every day and provides resources so you feel prepared and in control.
txt-pregnancy-end-healthscore-info-body-:
You might need a little extra support. 

Hold tight — you’re nearly through the questions. We’ll help you find additional resources and the emotional support you need.

For immediate help, contact [Postpartum Support International (PSI)](https://www.postpartum.net/get-help/?utm_source=NaturalCycles&utm_medium=app), a 24-hour hotline dedicated to supporting mothers and families dealing with perinatal mental health issues.

txt-pregnancy-end-induction-info-body:
Induced labor can be challenging. It can lead to stronger and more frequent contractions that may increase your chance of medical intervention and discomfort.

Recovery after induced labor may involve longer hospital stays and increased fatigue.

Whether you have had your labor induced or not, you’ve just been through something incredible. So, be gentle with yourself. It might take a little while to regain your strength and fully heal.

txt-venus-nudge-card-body: Be part of important research on contraceptive effectiveness and receive up to $260, plus your subscription reimbursed.
txt-venus-nudge-modal-body:
At Natural Cycles, we constantly monitor our effectiveness rates as a birth control method to ensure our claims always reflect your reality.

That’s why we are recruiting women who will be using the Natural Cycles app to prevent pregnancy for the whole upcoming year, and are anticipating being sexually active at least once per month.

**Why participate?**

You'll not only contribute to science but also receive compensation for your time. You can receive up to **$260 in Amazon gift cards** and reimbursement of your annual NC° subscription. 🎁

**What happens if I agree to participate?**

If you choose to join the VENUS Study, you’ll be asked to **log daily vaginal sex data** in the app for **one year**. The key is entering your data consistently and without much delay.

You’ll find full details in the [Information Sheet](https://www.datocms-assets.com/21281/1769528697-venus-information-sheet.pdf), participation is entirely voluntary.

Every participant makes a difference. **So, are you in**?
txt-venus-nudge-modal-title: The VENUS Study: Advance women’s health, and get rewarded ❣️

txt-zzz-bad-answer--1--body: It looks like you measured outside your normal wake up window. You should exclude your temperature if you’ve slept +/- 2 hours outside your wake up window.
txt-zzz-bad-answer--2--body: It looks like you may have snoozed or spent some time awake before measuring.  It’s best to exclude your temperature if you don’t measure soon after waking.
txt-zzz-bad-answer--3--body: It looks like you got up and out of bed before taking your temperature. If this happens you select exclude temperature.
txt-zzz-feedback-q1: 1. Did the tool help you decide if you slept differently than usual?
txt-zzz-good-answer-body:
If you measured within the +/- 2 hours of your normal wake-up window, didn’t snooze, and didn’t get out of bed before measuring, you don’t need to exclude your temperature.

Don’t worry if you get up during the night. It’s measuring at the same time in the morning that’s important.

It doesn’t matter if you moved around a bit in bed. As long as you didn’t get up before measuring, there’s no need to exclude your temperature today.

whoop-account-your-account-info:
You have connected your NC° account with your WHOOP account to import data from your WHOOP account to the Natural Cycles app. These data imports happen automatically when you open your WHOOP app each day. If you would like to terminate this data import from WHOOP to Natural Cycles, please click “Disconnect WHOOP account” below.  

This is a one-way integration, which means that any data you log on the Natural Cycles app will not sync with the WHOOP app. Always refer to the NC° app for Daily Fertility Status.  

When your accounts are connected, WHOOP and NC° may share limited account information to help troubleshoot and resolve technical issues.

The NC° Fertility Algorithm requires access to WHOOP data to deliver your daily fertility status and insights. When prompted, please allow all data sharing. 

Your NC° data is secure and isn't shared back to WHOOP.

yourBaby-text--10:
No longer an embryo, your baby has now become a fetus...but you can call it a prettier name if you wish. 💜
This week it reaches about the size of a kumquat. All of your baby’s vital organs have formed! Nevertheless, many of them will need a little more time to develop before becoming fully functional. As the first, most delicate phase of development comes to an end, your baby becomes a little less vulnerable to toxins. But this doesn’t mean that you should stop paying attention to what you put into your body!

Your baby now trains its arms and legs and has plenty of space to move around in the amniotic sac. The sac now contains about 100 ml/3.4 ounces of amniotic fluid, about the size of a glass of water. This provides nutrition and insulates and protects your baby from shocks.
yourBaby-text--11:
Your baby, as big as a lime, is growing and changing at incredible speed. Its head is now about half the size of its entire body, while it will be around ¼ of its length at birth. 

The reproductive system continues maturing, and a couple of weeks ago it started differentiating between male and female. Your baby’s sex was determined at conception, by the X or Y chromosome carried by the sperm. The egg can only bring an X chromosome, so it is technically the father who determines the sex of the children.

If the embryo has one X chromosome and one Y, it will be male, produce testosterone, and develop testicles, a prostate, and a penis. If the embryo has two X chromosomes, it will be female and will grow a uterus, a vagina, and ovaries. A baby girl is born with one to two million eggs that will begin to mature at puberty.
yourBaby-text--12:
Your baby looks more and more like a little human, about the size of a fig. This is the final week of the first trimester, and your baby’s vital systems continue to develop and gradually prepare to take over their functions. 
The stomach muscles and intestines are starting to learn typical digestion contractions, and the first tooth germs appear.

The nervous system has matured enough for your baby to instinctively move in response to a poke to your belly or a sudden movement of your body. Most of these reflexes, such as sucking, grabbing, stepping, and swimming, have most probably developed during human evolution to increase a baby’s chance of survival and help parents bond with their newborns. 

At this stage, your baby’s growth is fully supported by the placenta, which has fully taken over the task of providing oxygen and nutrients and of regulating pregnancy hormone levels.
yourBaby-text--13:
The first trimester of your pregnancy is almost over for you and your baby. Your baby’s proportions are slowly changing, with the head becoming smaller and adjusting to the size of the rest of its body. The size from head to bottom is now comparable to a lemon.

Vocal cords have formed, but have not been put to use yet. The skeleton is developing, at first with flexible bones made from cartilage. The bones will grow longer and thicker thanks to the calcium transferred from your body through the placenta, and will eventually turn into hard bone tissue.

Your little baby is also gaining strength! 💪 The neck is now strong enough for your fetus to move its head.
An ultrasound may already be able to reveal the sex, but the result may still be uncertain so many health care professionals prefer to wait a few weeks longer.
yourBaby-text--14:
Your baby is now about the size of a peach. Hair follicles start developing on its scalp and skin, but hair hasn’t begun to grow yet. To practice for life on the outside, your baby is moving around in your womb, although you cannot feel it yet as there is still plenty of free room in the amniotic sac. 

Your baby sucks its thumb to prepare for suckling after birth. It waves its arms and legs, practices walking, bends its back, and turns its head. The nose, with little nostrils, the mouth, and the eyelids are all in place. Facial expressions begin to take shape, starting with very simple reflexes such as stretching the lip or lifting an eyebrow. 

For now, these movements are only instinctive muscle contractions. It will take a little longer for your baby to learn to use its face to express emotions the way we do.
yourBaby-text--15:
This week your baby grows to the size of an orange. After the appearance of hair follicles, your baby is now growing a thin layer of fine, soft, unpigmented hair, known as lanugo. This prototype of hair covers the entire body, keeping it warm until the layer of fat beneath the skin has developed. 

It also protects your baby’s delicate skin that is immersed in the amniotic fluid. The lanugo will shed and grow back a few times until the third trimester when it normally disappears permanently. Some babies still show traces of it when they are born, and gradually lose them during their first few weeks of life. 

At birth, your baby will have temporary hair, usually softer, thinner, and sometimes lighter in color. It will take a few months -- or even years -- before you get to know your child’s true hair color!
yourBaby-text--16:
Your baby still grows very quickly and is by now as big as an avocado. Its arms and legs are now fully developed, with perfectly functional muscles and joints. A layer of brown body fat starts being produced under the skin, helping your baby to keep the right temperature.

Your baby’s sensory organs are getting ready to function. Its eyes started to develop very early, around week 4, when the optical nerves formed from a group of brain cells. All of the other parts, such as the lens and retina, grow throughout the first and early second trimester. Around this week the eyes finally become sensitive to light, and even though your baby’s eyelids are still sealed, its eyes already start to follow bright lights filtering through your body.
yourBaby-text--17:
The baby has grown to approximately the size of a turnip. Its heart gets stronger and stronger, now pumping around 24 liters/6.3 gallons of blood each day. Its hair and body fat continue to grow. The sensory organs keep developing. The ears have evolved enough for your baby to hear its very first sounds, such as your heart beating, your stomach growling, and your lungs breathing. 

Your baby’s hearing capacity is still very limited, and it will take several more weeks before your baby starts moving in reaction to sounds. Even then, your body and the amniotic fluid surrounding your baby muffle and distort the sounds coming from the outside world, like water does when you swim beneath the surface. 

The clearest sound your baby will pick up is your voice, which is amplified by your body and resonates within the womb. Studies have shown that the heartbeat of a baby slows down when their mother is speaking!
yourBaby-text--18:
Your baby’s limbs are growing in size to catch up with the rest of the body, which is now about as big as an artichoke. As muscles grow stronger and joints keep developing, your baby’s range of motion increases. Your baby now has a clear rhythm of activity and rest throughout the day, called circadian rhythm. 
However, you and your baby are not on the same schedule. 😉 

During the day, your baby mainly sleeps, cradled by your movements, and tends to become more active during the night while you rest. Don’t worry if you haven’t felt anything yet! There is still quite a bit of space left around your baby, so this is perfectly normal at this stage of your pregnancy, especially if you’re expecting your first child. If you already have children, the muscles in your womb are softer, so you might become aware of your baby’s first movements a little earlier.
yourBaby-text--19:
Your baby is growing at an amazing pace, and now reaches the size of a mango. The reproductive system is now clearly different for boys and girls, although if you are having a boy his testicles haven’t descended from the abdomen yet. A baby girl already has up to two million eggs in her ovaries! 

An ultrasound at this stage can tell you the sex of your baby if you don’t want to be surprised. Whatever the gender, your baby is now developing the vernix caseosa (“cheesy varnish” in Latin), which is a layer of white greasy wax that covers the skin. This wax will be produced by specialized cells until birth, and many newborns still show some of it. The vernix protects the delicate skin from the amniotic fluid, keeps it moist, provides heat insulation, and even facilitates the baby’s journey through the birth canal during delivery.
yourBaby-text--2:
Your adventure starts here! This week a mature egg cell has been released by one of your ovaries during ovulation and has started moving through the fallopian tubes towards your uterus. A sperm cell travels through the tubes towards the egg, a journey that can take anywhere from a few hours to a few days.

When the sperm meets the egg, together they turn into something brand new called a zygote. The zygote is a combination of both you and your partner, and it is at this early stage that the sex of your baby is determined.
yourBaby-text--20:
Congratulations, you and your baby are halfway through your pregnancy! 🎉
Around this time it is common to do an ultrasound, so you can see your baby if you haven’t already. Your baby, now as big as a banana, is moving more and more and gaining strength to prepare for birth. As your baby grows bigger, you will be able to feel its activity. 

At first, it won’t be all kicks and punches but rather a feeling of fluttering, like butterflies in your stomach. The feeling can be localized high up in your belly, or as low as your pubic bone. It will take a while before the pattern of movement becomes regular enough for you to track it. 
If you haven’t felt anything, there is no need to worry. It is not uncommon to feel the first movements until around week 24. 

The development of the nervous system and the sensory organs -- vision, taste, smell, touch -- continue at a fast pace.
yourBaby-text--21:
So far your baby has been smaller in size than the placenta, but it has now finally outgrown it! It has become about as big as an endive. The space in the amniotic sac is slowly getting more constrained, although there is still some free space left. By now your baby resembles a miniature newborn, it has a little face with lips and eyebrows. The eyelids are shut but this doesn’t stop your baby from practicing facial expressions, as you may have seen in your mid-pregnancy ultrasound. 

The digestive system is getting ready to function, even though your body still provides all the nutrients. Your baby continuously swallows and digests amniotic fluid, and produces a dark waste product known as meconium. This is often found at the first diaper change after birth before your baby starts digesting milk.
yourBaby-text--22:
Your baby now has approximately the same body proportions as a newborn, and about the size of a bell pepper. It is still quite lean compared to the chubby baby you will get to know at birth since much of its fat hasn’t been produced yet. Your baby’s skin and all its layers are almost fully developed, but the lack of fat makes it look translucent, showing the web of blood vessels underneath. It is also wrinkled, your baby is constantly immersed in the amniotic fluid. 

Most of the pigments are missing, the hair is almost white, and the irises have no color yet. 
Babies of all ethnicities look very similar at this stage. The future color of your child’s skin, hair, and eyes were determined at conception as it is genetically inherited from the parents, but it doesn’t show yet. It can even keep changing after your baby is born.
yourBaby-text--23:
By now your baby, as big as a grapefruit, is almost fully formed with most of its features in place. The sensory organs continue developing, making it more aware of the surrounding world. As it's hearing capability improves, your baby becomes familiar with the tone of your voice and the louder sounds of your daily life such as a dog barking.

The taste sense is also developing. The taste organs branched off the nervous system during the first ten weeks of pregnancy. Later on, the nerves connected to the taste buds appeared on the surface of the tongue, enabling your baby to feel the five basic tastes of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. However, until your baby is born it will only experience the slightly salty taste of the amniotic fluid and maybe some very faint flavor from the food you eat passed from your bloodstream into the liquid.
yourBaby-text--24:
Your baby, now about the size of a small ear of corn, is gradually becoming mature enough for the outside world. 
Balance organs have developed in the inner ear.

One of the last vital systems to develop and start functioning is the respiratory system.
It started forming very early on, when your baby was still an embryo, with the appearance of the first simple airways and lung buds. These buds grow like a tree, splitting into smaller and smaller branches ending with the little chambers where breathing will occur upon birth. 

At this stage, the lungs start to produce the substance that will enable them to expand and breathe, known as surfactant. Unlike other organs, the lungs will not begin to function before your baby is born. Even so, your baby will regularly expand and contract its chest, breathing amniotic fluid to practice.
yourBaby-text--25:
By this week your baby has become about as big a rutabaga. Safe in your womb, it will still grow bigger and stronger while its brain and sensory organs continue developing. Your baby’s nostrils are almost complete and are about to open. Through them and through its mouth the baby will start breathing small quantities of amniotic fluid to practice inhaling and exhaling chest movements and facilitate the formation of the lungs. 

As its sense of smell develops along with the taste, your baby will also be able to better perceive the substances in the amniotic fluid, including faint scents of the foods you eat, especially the ones with the strongest flavor. The sense of smell is very important for newborns. Together with the memory of the voices from the womb, it will help them recognize and bond with their parents. 💜
yourBaby-text--26:
Your baby, now as big as a scallion, has both eyebrows and eyelashes now. So far the eyelids were sealed shut to protect the eyes from the feeble light filtering into the darkness of your womb, but this week or the next your baby might open them and blink for the first time! 

At this stage its eyesight is not well developed yet, so your baby won’t see much more than bright blurs and shadows. Vision is the sense that takes the longest to develop. Your baby can now hear, see, smell, and taste. Since a very early stage, your baby is also capable of feeling touch through its skin. It touches the womb, grabs its own feet and the umbilical cord, rubs its face. Your baby also responds to your touch, and you may have already felt it kicking when you push on your belly!
yourBaby-text--27:
This is the last week of the second trimester of your pregnancy, you and your baby are about to enter the last trimester. Only one-third of these long nine months is left before you two get to meet each other! 
Your baby is now about the size of a head of lettuce. Its vital organs are now all in place, although some of them, such as the lungs, need a little more time before they can function. 

In the next three months, your fetus will continue preparing for the outside world by gaining weight and getting stronger and more aware with each passing day. As the layer of body fat gets thicker beneath its skin, the baby gradually loses its wrinkly appearance and looks more and more like a newborn. Even more so when it sucks its thumb!
yourBaby-text--28:
Your baby has reached the size of a zucchini. 

Along with the other organs, your baby’s nervous system is evolving quickly. All the elements are already in place, developed from a little group of nerve cells that differentiated when your baby was still an embryo. The various parts of the brain have formed and are progressively gaining control over movements, body temperature, hormone production, sleep, thirst, hunger, and vital functions such as breathing and heartbeat. 

The nerve cells, called neurons, connect to each other creating synapses and develops your baby’s capacity to think, feel, and remember. Brainwave activity could now be detected, and when your baby sleeps, which happens around 90% of the time, it reaches the REM phase. This means that your baby is dreaming!
yourBaby-text--29:
Your baby grows bigger and bigger and is now the size of an eggplant. As it gains more weight the free space in the amniotic sac gradually shrinks. At the same time, your baby becomes stronger and more active, which means that you should now feel regular movement in your belly and be able to keep track of them. You might even feel your baby hiccup sometimes, like a rhythmic popping in your belly. This is due to the amniotic fluid it swallows and inhales, and is quite normal.  

Your baby also continues to practice its breathing. The inhaling and exhaling rhythm becomes more regular with time and the lungs continue producing surfactant, the substance that enables them to expand and breathe once your baby is born.
yourBaby-text--3:
This is the very first week of your pregnancy and the beginning of the journey that you will take with your new baby! It is still very early so you might not even know that you are pregnant yet. You will probably notice towards the end of this week, or next week if your cycle is a little longer when your period would normally be due.

A few days ago your egg was fertilized by a sperm cell, forming the single-cell zygote carrying the merged DNA of the two parents. Your zygote continues traveling through the fallopian tubes and reaches your uterus, which has already prepared to receive it. During this journey, which takes between five and six days, the cell will divide several times, and eventually start to differentiate. Your zygote has now become an embryo! 🎉
yourBaby-text--30:
Your baby has reached about the size of a large cauliflower. After many weeks of incredible development, its growth is finally slowing down. The quantity of amniotic fluid, which kept increasing throughout the pregnancy until about two weeks ago, is starting to decline. 
Right before delivery, you will see this liquid when your water breaks, which is when the amniotic sac is ruptured to allow your baby to move through the birth canal. The fluid is clear or pale yellow and keeps the temperature level around your baby, protecting it like a cushion from sudden movements and shocks. 

It facilitates the development of the skeleton, the muscles, and the digestive system. It also contains nutrients and waste products, such as your baby’s urine and the shed lanugo.
yourBaby-text--31:
Your baby, now as big as a cabbage, continues to gain weight and strength, receiving oxygen and nutrients from your blood through the placenta and umbilical cord. These organs connect the baby’s circulatory system to your own, without ever letting the blood mix. 

The umbilical cord, your baby’s lifeline, develops throughout your pregnancy and is approximately the same length as your baby. At birth, your baby will still be connected to the placenta through the cord. The cord will then close so that the blood flow stops naturally. Your healthcare professional will usually wait a few minutes after the baby is delivered until the cord stops pulsing, then clamp it and cut it. Your baby will not feel any pain, as the cord has no nerves. 

The stump that remains will dry out naturally and fall off after a few days, leaving a healed navel.
yourBaby-text--32:
Your baby is now about the size of a cantaloupe and despite the incredible expansion of your uterus, it is getting quite cramped in there. The lack of space in the amniotic sac restricts its movements and can change the way they feel in your body. Your baby can no longer flip and turn as freely as before, but still has bursts of activity where it squirms, stretches, and gives sudden taps, jabs, and kicks. 

These movements can be triggered by external stimuli such as loud sounds, motion, or by the higher sugar levels in your blood after you ate a snack or a meal. In the next couple of weeks, your baby might already start turning and descending towards your lower abdomen, although sometimes it happens later on.
yourBaby-text--33:
Your baby is now approximately the size of a squash.

Some of the baby’s vital systems are getting their finishing touches before birth. As its body fat increases your baby’s skin, which used to be almost transparent, finally becomes opaque. The skeleton grows and gets harder, although the skull is still immature.

Your baby’s head remains soft and malleable since the plates of bone that make up the skull haven’t fused together. This flexibility will allow the head to mold during the delivery, facilitating the passage through the narrow birth canal. This is why it is very common for newborns to have a slightly misshapen head, especially after a vaginal birth. The flexible skull also allows for the rapid growth of the brain. The gaps between plates will naturally close when your baby is about 18 months old.
yourBaby-text--34:
Your baby now is growing to the size of a pineapple.

Along with all the vital organs, the immune system has been evolving in the past months and will continue doing so. The first prototype of the immune system appeared very early on in your pregnancy, around week 9, when a group of cells divided and transformed into white blood cells. These are the cells that are in charge of fighting viruses, bacteria, and other invaders attacking the body.

During the following weeks and months, the baby’s immune defenses have become stronger by receiving help from your own as you share your antibodies through the placenta. At this stage, and even more so at birth, your baby’s immune system can already take care of protecting it from infections.
yourBaby-text--35:
Your baby is now as big as a spaghetti squash, and won't grow much more than a few centimeters/a couple of inches in length, although it will keep gaining weight until birth. By now it already nearly fills the entire uterus and will become more and more cramped.
Your baby’s hearing capacity is now as mature as it will be at birth. 

If you are expecting a baby boy, his testicles may be descending from his abdomen, but this can also occur later on in the pregnancy or even after birth. 
Your baby is almost ready to meet the outside world.

If you are expecting twins your pregnancy might end up being a few weeks shorter than the average single gestation, and your babies will be already considered full term at week 37. In this case, you may already be very close to giving birth!
yourBaby-text--36:
Your baby has grown to the size of a papaya.

Most of your baby’s organs are now functioning, and the lungs are almost ready to expand and breathe the air. The skin is now softer and opaque, and the lanugo is falling off. 

Although this is different for every pregnancy, your baby may have started moving down towards your pelvis, especially if this is your first child. If you have given birth before this may happen later on or even just before labor. 

Around this week most babies have moved into the head-down position that facilitates the birthing process. Your healthcare professional will be able to tell you if your baby has moved into this position. In some cases, this flip does not happen and the baby remains in what is known as the breech presentation, with its bottom or feet facing the birth canal. Your healthcare professional may then try to turn the baby.
yourBaby-text--37:
This is the week that your pregnancy reaches term, although it’s still on the early side. There is quite a lot of variation in the length of normal pregnancies, and about half of all deliveries happen between week 37 and 39, so your baby may be arriving soon. 

In your womb, the baby keeps growing and is now the size of romaine lettuce. It will gain approximately 30 g/1 ounce a day until it is born. It continues shedding the lanugo and losing the vernix caseosa, the wax covering its soft skin. Both the lanugo and vernix end up in the amniotic fluid and are swallowed and digested by the baby together with other waste products. The very first feeding will occur very soon after delivery. Many newborns spontaneously seek the breast to feed as soon as they are in skin-to-skin contact with their mother.
yourBaby-text--38:
Your baby keeps growing in your womb and now reaches about the size of a winter melon. Your healthcare professional may already have an indication of your baby’s size before birth by measuring the fundal height, which is the distance between your pubic bone and the top of your uterus. 

Many factors can influence the weight of a baby at birth. Baby boys are on average slightly bigger than baby girls. As weight gain in the womb is quite steep, the general rule is that the longer they have been in there, the bigger the newborn will be at birth. Ethnicity is also a relevant factor, newborns of South Asian, Chinese, or African American heritage weigh on average a little less than those of European origin. The mother’s age, diet, weight, and health before and during pregnancy, as well as whether she had already other children, all influence the baby’s weight at birth.
yourBaby-text--39:
Hooray! 🎉 You and your baby have reached full term! This means that your baby, now as big as a watermelon, is ready for the outside world.

A lot of things happen before and during delivery. The amniotic sac breaks and releases the amniotic fluid, allowing your baby to start moving towards the birth canal. Thanks to the strong labor contractions your cervix, the lowest part of your uterus, stretches and opens to more than 10 cm/4 inches. Your baby descends, typically head first, and during the descent, its head and body rotate to pass through the tight space of your pelvic bones and muscles. Once your baby is born, your body still needs to expel the placenta, attached to the umbilical cord. 

Then the most amazing part of your journey starts. You get to hold your new baby and bonding continues through the scent and feel of your skin. 💜
yourBaby-text--4:
Your embryo has reached the womb and prepares to attach to the endometrium, which is the inner lining of the uterus. This process is called implantation. The endometrium becomes thicker and blood flow is increased, as it prepares to provide oxygen and nutrition to the embryo. At this stage, the embryo is called a blastocyst. 

The embryo is still only a tiny ball the size of a poppy seed. The cells, now a few hundred, continue to rapidly divide and differentiate. The parts that will become the yolk sac and the placenta also start to form. They will provide nourishment and oxygen, eliminate waste products, and regulate the temperature until your baby is born.
yourBaby-text--40:
You and the world may be ready for your baby, but babies can be stubborn even before they’re born. The due date is predicted for this week as the average pregnancy is 40 weeks (280 days) long, but there is quite a lot of variation and only about 5% of deliveries happen on the predicted due date.

You may have to be patient and wait a little longer, as about one-third of all births happen later than the predicted due date. Whatever the date, the incredible journey that started nine long months ago, when egg and sperm met, is close to an end. Labor and birth will definitely be hard work, but you will soon get to hold your own little human for the very first time, a new life that will grow and discover the world together with you. 🌎
yourBaby-text--41:
Hang in there! If your baby is still cozied up in your womb, there is no need to stress even though this can be a tiring and nerve-wracking time. In the meantime, your baby is growing bigger and stronger. Its nails are growing, as well as the hair, although some newborns are completely bald. 

One-third of all pregnancies last longer than the due date. Your baby is not yet postterm, but your healthcare professional may want to keep in touch with you to make sure that all is well. If possible, they will most likely prefer to wait for natural labor.
yourBaby-text--5:
Your embryo continues changing very rapidly, in both shape and size. By the end of this week, it will be the size of a sesame seed and have the shape of an oval, rather than a ball. The ends of this oval will become your baby’s head and bottom.   

The cells inside of the embryo have started to form three layers of cells that will later develop into your baby’s organs. 
The first layer will develop into your baby’s nervous system, ears, eyes, and skin. 
The second layer will develop into your baby’s lungs, bladder, and digestive tract. 
The third layer will develop into your baby’s heart and circulatory system, blood, kidneys, and muscles. 

The spinal cord, a first prototype of the heart, and the inner genitals start appearing.
yourBaby-text--6:
Your embryo is growing quickly, doubling in size with each passing week. It is now as big as a lentil and looks more like a tadpole than a human being with a primitive head and a little tail that will eventually disappear. Arms and legs start to form, sprouting like buds along your baby’s body. Eyes, nose, and mouth could already be made out, too.

The first organ to start functioning is the heart, already beating at the impressive rate of 100-160 beats per minute. At this stage, it is made up of two tubes that will fuse together and develop into rudimentary atria and ventricles, the four cavities that pump blood.

It may already be possible for an early ultrasound to pick up your baby’s heartbeat, but it is still quite difficult. In any case, you might have to wait a little longer as the first ultrasound is often not scheduled until week eight or nine.
yourBaby-text--7:
Your baby, now the size of a blueberry, is still technically an embryo but is growing in size and complexity every day. Your baby’s facial features, such as eyelids, nose, nostrils, and ears, are gradually forming. The arms and legs continue growing, while the tail becomes less noticeable before disappearing completely. 

The left and right heart chambers are pumping blood with more and more strength, which makes the heartbeat a little easier to detect on ultrasound. Seeing the baby’s heartbeat is usually a good reassurance that the pregnancy is healthy and all is going well.

The nervous system grows from a simple tube to a complex structure, with the appearance of a prototype of the brain. Nervous cells multiply and evolve into neurons. The respiratory, digestive, urinary, and reproductive systems take shape.
yourBaby-text--8:
Your baby has now approximately reached the size of a kidney bean. Its organs continue developing, and little webbed fingers and toes appear on its hands and feet. The tail is almost completely gone, and the embryo starts resembling a tiny human being, even though the head is still much larger with respect to the body than it will be at birth. Genitals start to form, but are still immature and look the same for both male and female. 

In some countries, an ultrasound scan is done in the first trimester between week 8 and 12. The purpose is to confirm and date the pregnancy, make sure that everything is progressing well, and determine if you are expecting a single baby or multiples. You should also be able to hear your baby’s heartbeat for the first time! 💓
yourBaby-text--9:
Your baby, now about as big as a cherry, is still growing quickly. The major organs are almost developed.
Fingers and toes grow longer and lose their webbing, elbows and knees can now bend, and the head becomes more round. Facial features such as the nose and chin become more pronounced, and the eyes are almost fully formed beneath the shut eyelids. The optic nerves, which belong to the nervous system, were the first to develop a few weeks ago. By now the retina has formed.

This is the thin layer of tissue lining the back of the eye, sensitive to light. Your baby’s eye color was determined at conception when the DNA of egg and sperm merged, but it will show up quite a bit later and will keep changing even after birth.
